Cleanup function aborts in-flight request when query changes or unmounts
Loading state visible while fetching
Error state caught and displayed gracefully
Empty query does not trigger fetch
hints: Inside useEffect: const controller = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal }) ... return () => controller.abort();
Catch AbortError: if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setError(err.message);
drills.why: Timed build, roughly 20 min.

drills.title: Tell me about yourself — the 30-second version
drills.hook: The first question is not a biography request. It is a positioning question, and the answer sets the frame for every question after it.
drills.deepDive: A strong answer is three beats and under 45 seconds. (1) Where you are now, in one line — role, stack, scale. (2) The one thing that makes you unusual, stated as a capability rather than a claim. (3) Why this role, connected to something specific about the team or the work. Then stop.
drills.spokenDefence: "I build front-end systems in React — most recently a spec-first workflow where the tooling grades the work rather than the developer marking their own homework. What I bring beyond the stack is that I design the process around the failure mode, not just the feature."
acceptanceCriteria: Under 45 seconds spoken
No college-to-present chronology
Contains at least one concrete number (scale, users, time, latency)
Ends on why this company, not on a generic goal
hints: Three beats: where you are now · what makes you unusual · why this role. Nothing else.
Replace every adjective with a fact. Not "passionate about performance" — "cut a 2.4s LCP to 900ms".
End on the role, not on yourself. The last sentence should point at them.
drills.why: It is asked in every round, by every interviewer, and it is the only answer you can prepare word-for-word without it sounding rehearsed.

drills.title: A time you disagreed with a technical decision
drills.hook: They are not asking whether you were right. They are asking whether you can disagree without creating wreckage, and whether you can execute a decision you lost.
drills.deepDive: The shape: you had a different view on an architectural or process choice · you grounded your argument in data/constraints rather than taste · you stated your case clearly · a decision was made · you committed fully either way. If you won, the victory was quiet; if you lost, you did not drag your feet.
drills.spokenDefence: "We were choosing between writing a custom virtualised list and using an off-the-shelf library for a 10k-item view. I advocated the library because our edge cases were standard. The lead wanted custom to avoid bundle weight. I ran a spike, measured the bundle delta at 8kB, and we went with the library. If we had stayed with custom, I would have owned the tests."
acceptanceCriteria: Situation is technical, not personal
The disagreement was resolved with evidence, not authority
Result shows full commitment to the outcome
Under 60 seconds spoken
hints: The disagreement must be technical or process, never interpersonal.
Show the evidence you brought, not just the opinion you held.
The ending must show commitment, whether your view was taken or not.
drills.why: Seniority is mostly how you handle disagreement. A junior engineer treats it as a fight to win; a senior engineer treats it as a search for the cheapest correct answer.

drills.title: A time you caused or handled a production outage
drills.hook: A candidate who has never broken production has either never shipped anything or does not know when they broke it.
drills.deepDive: The answer that loses the interview is the fake failure: "I worked too hard" or "a third-party API went down". A real failure has a real blast radius, your own contribution acknowledged without hiding behind the team, and a permanent change made to the system so the same mistake is impossible.
drills.spokenDefence: "I pushed an un-memoized selector into a shared hook that caused a re-render cascade on every keypress in our main form. We caught it in staging telemetry before deploy. The fix was two lines; the real work was adding an ESLint rule so the pattern fails in CI for anyone else."
acceptanceCriteria: A real cost is named
Your own share is owned without blaming others
Most of the answer is the fix, not the failure
The fix is systemic — a check, a test, a process — not "I was more careful"
hints: Pick a real mistake, not a humblebrag.
Spend 20% on the mistake, 80% on the response and the systemic fix.
The fix must be a mechanism (linter, test, alert, runbook), not "I was more careful".
drills.why: Interviewers look for psychological safety and systemic thinking. Hiding a failure signals risk; explaining what you fixed in the system signals reliability.

drills.title: Walk me through a project you are proud of
drills.hook: This is a technical question wearing behavioural clothes. They are looking for the decisions, the constraints and the trade-offs — not the feature list.
drills.deepDive: Structure it as: the problem and who had it · the constraint that made it hard · two decisions you made and what you gave up for each · how you knew it worked. The trade-off sentences are the whole answer.
drills.spokenDefence: "Problem, constraint, two trade-offs, evidence it worked. Then stop and let them pick which thread to pull."
acceptanceCriteria: Opens with the problem, not the stack
Names a real constraint
Contains two explicit trade-offs with what was given up
Ends with a measurement
hints: Lead with the problem and the person who had it, never with the stack.
Two trade-offs, each with what you gave up. That is the scored part.
Have a number for "how you knew it worked".
drills.why: The longest answer you will give, and the one where interviewers form their technical opinion of you.

drills.title: Do you have any questions for us?
drills.hook: "No, I think you covered everything" is the single most expensive sentence in the interview. It is the last thing they hear, and it reads as indifference.
drills.deepDive: Prepare three, and ask two. Good questions reveal what you pay attention to: how work is decided, what failure looks like on this team, what the person answering wishes were different.
drills.spokenDefence: "What does a piece of work look like when it goes badly here — and what usually caused it?" It is disarming, specific, and the answer tells you whether to accept the offer.
acceptanceCriteria: Three questions written
None answerable from the careers page
At least one is about failure or difficulty, not perks
One slot reserved to reference something said in the room
hints: Three prepared, two asked. Never zero.
One question must reference something they said in this conversation.
Nothing answerable from the careers page; no compensation in a technical round.
drills.why: It is the last impression, it is entirely within your control, and it is the one nobody rehearses.

drills.title: Handling a question you cannot answer
drills.hook: You will be asked something you do not know. The answer is not a guess, and it is not "I don't know" full stop. It is a bounded, honest reach.
drills.deepDive: The three-part move: say what you do know that is adjacent · say plainly where your knowledge stops · say how you would find out. That reads as calibrated, and calibration is what senior means.
drills.spokenDefence: "I have not used Server Components in production. What I know is the boundary — they run on the server, ship no JS, and cannot hold state. Where I would need to check is caching. I would start with the React docs and build a small route."
acceptanceCriteria: Adjacent knowledge stated before the gap
The edge of knowledge is named explicitly
A concrete method for finding out
No bluffing, no apologising
hints: Adjacent knowledge first — it shows the shape of what you do have.
Name the edge explicitly. "Where I would need to check is…" is a senior sentence.
Finish with the method, not an apology.
drills.why: Every technical round contains at least one. How you handle it is worth more than the answer would have been.

drills.title: Stack vs Heap: Primitives & References
drills.hook: Primitives are compared by value. Objects are compared by their memory address (pointer).
drills.deepDive: When you assign `let a = 10; let b = a;`, a literal copy of 10 is made. But when you do `let a = {}; let b = a;`, only the pointer is copied. Mutating `b` will mutate `a` because they point to the identical heap address.
drills.spokenDefence: "Primitives are immutable values living on the call stack. Objects are mutable structures in the heap. In React, this is why we must never mutate an object in state directly—React compares pointers using Object.is, and if the pointer hasn't changed, it assumes the data hasn't changed, causing stale UI bugs."
acceptanceCriteria: Asserts primitive isolation (p1 remains 5).
Asserts object reference mutation (obj1.val becomes 99).

mcq.q: What is the output of `{} === {}`?
mcq.why: Each `{}` creates a new object in memory with a distinct pointer. Distinct pointers are never strictly equal.

drills.title: Shallow vs Deep Copying (The Nested Trap)
drills.hook: Spread syntax `{...obj}` creates a shallow copy. It only clones the outermost shell.
drills.deepDive: If you have an object with nested children, `const clone = { ...obj }` creates a new pointer for the root, but the nested children still share the exact same pointers as the original. If you mutate `clone.nested.x`, you mutate the original. To fix this, you must either spread nested levels too, or use `structuredClone()`.
drills.spokenDefence: "When building reducers or state updates, a shallow copy using spread is usually enough. But if the data structure is heavily nested, mutating a deep property on a shallow clone mutates the original state, breaking time-travel debugging and causing cross-component side effects. I reach for structuredClone for complex nested updates."
acceptanceCriteria: Creates a shallow copy via spread.
Creates a deep copy via structuredClone.
Proves the original is mutated by shallow clone but protected by deep clone.

mcq.q: What does structuredClone NOT copy?
mcq.why: Functions, DOM Nodes, and Error objects cannot be cloned by structuredClone and will throw a DataCloneError.

drills.title: The 4 Equalities: Object.is & NaN
drills.hook: JavaScript has 4 ways to compare equality. React relies heavily on `Object.is`.
drills.deepDive:
1) `==` (Loose) coerces types.
2) `===` (Strict) blocks coercion, but `NaN !== NaN` and `+0 === -0`.
3) `Object.is` is like strict, but fixes math bugs: `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true, and `Object.is(+0, -0)` is false.
4) `SameValueZero` is what Maps and Sets use under the hood.
drills.spokenDefence: "React's dependency arrays and useState bailouts use Object.is algorithm under the hood, not ===. This is why if you update a state variable from NaN to NaN, React will NOT re-render, whereas a strict equality check would think they are different and trigger a re-render."
acceptanceCriteria: Logs NaN comparison using === and Object.is
Logs signed zero comparison using === and Object.is

mcq.q: How does React compare dependencies in `useEffect`?
mcq.why: React uses Object.is polyfill (is() in the React source code) to prevent re-renders when setState is called with identical values, strictly handling NaN correctly.

drills.title: Event Loop: Macrotasks vs Microtasks
drills.hook: Promises resolve before SetTimeout. Microtasks beat Macrotasks.
drills.deepDive: When synchronous code finishes, the JS engine checks the Microtask queue (Promises, MutationObserver). It drains the ENTIRE microtask queue until it is empty. ONLY THEN does it look at the Macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI rendering).
drills.spokenDefence: "If an interviewer asks me to predict the output of nested setTimeouts and Promises, I isolate the queues. Synchronous code runs immediately. Promise .then() callbacks go to the Microtask queue which is drained exhaustively before the browser is allowed to render or process the Macrotask queue where setTimeout callbacks live."
acceptanceCriteria: Demonstrates sync execution.
Demonstrates Promise (Microtask) execution priority over setTimeout.

mcq.q: Which logs first? Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(1)); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);
mcq.why: Promise callbacks are microtasks. setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks. The microtask queue is always drained before the macrotask queue.

drills.title: Canceling REST API Requests with AbortController
drills.hook: When a component unmounts or a user types rapidly in a search box, lingering network requests cause race conditions and memory leaks.
drills.deepDive: `fetch()` takes an `abort` signal. The `AbortController` exposes a `.signal` to pass to fetch, and a `.abort()` method to immediately terminate the request. In React, you call `abort()` in the `useEffect` cleanup function to guarantee the request dies if the component unmounts or the effect re-runs.
drills.spokenDefence: "If an interviewer asks how to handle search debouncing or rapid navigation, I emphasize AbortController. Debouncing delays the start, but AbortController cancels the in-flight network request, freeing up the browser's connection pool and preventing stale data from overwriting fresh data if responses return out of order."
acceptanceCriteria: Creates AbortController instance.
Passes signal to fetch options.
Calls abort() in useEffect cleanup.

mcq.q: What error does fetch throw when aborted?
mcq.why: fetch rejects the Promise with a DOMException named "AbortError". You must catch this so your app doesn't crash.

drills.title: Closures & Stale State (The React Hooks Trap)
drills.hook: A closure "remembers" the variables in its lexical scope at the exact moment it was created.
drills.deepDive: When you create a function inside another function (like an event handler or useEffect inside a React component), it captures the state variables from that specific render pass. If the function is delayed (e.g., setTimeout) and state changes in the meantime, the function will still see the OLD (stale) state.
drills.spokenDefence: "A common React interview question is why a setTimeout inside a useEffect sees an old state value. I explain that React hooks rely on closures. Each render creates a new closure over the state variables of that render. A delayed function holds a reference to the environment of the render where it was created, not the latest one. To fix it, you either use a ref (which is mutable and survives renders) or functional state updates like `setCount(c => c + 1)`."
acceptanceCriteria: Demonstrates the stale closure problem.
Demonstrates how an object reference bypasses the closure trap.

mcq.q: If `count = 0` and you run: `setTimeout(() => console.log(count), 1000)`, then immediately `count = 99`, what logs?
mcq.why: The setTimeout callback forms a closure over the value of `count` (0) at the time it was declared.

drills.title: Lexical vs Dynamic: Arrow Functions & "this"
drills.hook: Regular functions determine this dynamically based on WHO called them. Arrow functions determine this lexically based on WHERE they were written.
drills.deepDive: Before arrow functions, passing a method as a callback (like `element.addEventListener('click', obj.method)`) would strip the object binding, and this would become the window or undefined. Arrow functions don't have their own this. They look up the scope chain just like any normal variable.
drills.spokenDefence: "When asked why we used to `bind(this)` in React class components, I explain dynamic execution context. A method passed as an event handler loses its instance context when invoked by the DOM. Arrow functions solved this because their this is lexically scoped to the enclosing class, permanently binding it to the instance."
acceptanceCriteria: Identifies the broken dynamic binding.
Fixes it using a lexical arrow function.

mcq.q: What does this refer to inside a global arrow function?
mcq.why: An arrow function in the global scope inherits this from the global scope, which is the Window object in a browser.

drills.title: The Debounced Search API
drills.hook: Mettl throws a curveball: 'Build a search bar that calls an API, but you cannot use React.' Can you survive?
drills.deepDive: A classic technical round trap. They want to see if you rely entirely on React hooks or if you actually understand the underlying browser mechanics. You must use a closure to hold the `timer` ID, `clearTimeout` on every keystroke, and invoke the network request only when the user stops typing.
drills.spokenDefence: 'Debouncing limits the rate at which a function fires. It’s crucial for performance on search inputs or window resizes. I implement it using a higher-order function that returns a closure; the closure tracks the timeout ID and resets it every time it's called before the delay expires.'
acceptanceCriteria: Should execute the function only once after rapid successive calls.

mcq.q: In a debounce function, why must the timer variable be declared OUTSIDE the returned inner function?
options: Because inner functions cannot declare variables.
So the variable persists in memory (closure) across multiple calls to the inner function.
To make it globally accessible to the window object.
mcq.why: If the timer was declared inside the returned function, it would be recreated as `undefined` on every keystroke, destroying the ability to clear the previous timeout.

drills.title: Polyfill: Array.prototype.reduce
drills.hook: If you don't know how `reduce` works under the hood, how can you trust it for complex data transformations?
drills.deepDive: Writing polyfills is the ultimate test of JS mastery. To build `reduce`, you must understand `this` (which points to the array calling the method), handle the optional `initialValue`, and iterate correctly, feeding the accumulator forward into the callback.
drills.spokenDefence: 'Writing a polyfill for reduce requires handling the execution context (`this`), managing the accumulator state, and treating the initial value correctly. If no initial value is provided, the first element of the array becomes the accumulator, and iteration starts from index 1.'
acceptanceCriteria: Should correctly accumulate values with and without an initial value.

mcq.q: Inside a polyfill function assigned to `Array.prototype.myMap = function() { ... }`, what does `this` refer to?
options: The array that the method was called on.
mcq.why: When a function is called as a method on an object (e.g., `[1,2,3].myMap()`), `this` binds to the object (the array) left of the dot.

drills.title: The Temporal Dead Zone (Hoisting)
drills.hook: Why does `var` give you `undefined` while `let` and `const` throw a ReferenceError? Welcome to the TDZ.
drills.deepDive: All declarations (even `let` and `const`) are hoisted to the top of their block scope in the Creation Phase. However, `var` is initialized with `undefined` immediately. `let` and `const` remain uninitialized in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) until the parser evaluates their assignment line. Accessing them before that throws a ReferenceError.
drills.spokenDefence: In an interview, explain that hoisting applies to all variable declarations, but the *initialization* behavior differs. Use this to explain why `var` is dangerous—it fails silently by returning `undefined`, whereas the TDZ in `let`/`const` forces a strict fail-fast error, preventing subtle runtime bugs.
acceptanceCriteria: Should correctly order variable declarations to avoid TDZ and undefined.

mcq.why: `var a` is hoisted and initialized to `undefined`. `let b` is hoisted but stays in the TDZ, so accessing it throws a ReferenceError.

drills.title: `this` Binding & Arrow Function Traps
drills.hook: Why does passing an object method as a callback log `undefined` or the global object instead of your target data?
drills.deepDive: In standard functions, `this` is dynamically bound based on *how* the function is invoked (the call site). When detached as a callback, it defaults to `undefined` (in strict mode) or `window`. Arrow functions do NOT possess their own `this` binding—they lexically capture `this` from the enclosing lexical execution context at definition time.
drills.spokenDefence: State clearly: 'Arrow functions do not bind their own `this`, `arguments`, `super`, or `new.target`. They inherit `this` from the parent scope. Standard functions bind `this` dynamically at invocation time unless explicitly bound using `.bind()`, `.call()`, or `.apply()`.'
acceptanceCriteria: Should preserve `this` context inside asynchronous callback.

mcq.why: Object literals do NOT create a new lexical scope. The arrow function captures `this` from the outer module or window scope, where `val` is undefined.

drills.title: Microtasks vs Macrotasks Execution Order
drills.hook: In what order do `setTimeout(..., 0)`, `Promise.resolve()`, `queueMicrotask`, and synchronous code execute?
drills.deepDive: The JavaScript runtime executes synchronous code on the Call Stack. When the Call Stack clears, the Event Loop processes the ENTIRE Microtask Queue (Promises, `queueMicrotask`, MutationObserver) before executing the NEXT SINGLE Macrotask (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O). If a microtask enqueues another microtask, it will starve the macrotask queue.
drills.spokenDefence: Explain: 'Microtasks have higher priority than macrotasks. The event loop drains the entire microtask queue at the end of each tick/macrotask, before yielding to the browser rendering phase or the next macrotask.'
acceptanceCriteria: Should execute with correct Event Loop priority.

mcq.why: Synchronous logs (1, 4) execute first. Then the Promise microtask (3) drains. Finally, the setTimeout macrotask (2) runs.

drills.title: The `var` Loop Closure Trap
drills.hook: Why does a `setTimeout` inside a `for (var i = 0; i < 3)` loop output `3, 3, 3` instead of `0, 1, 2`?
drills.deepDive: `var` is function-scoped, not block-scoped. So there is only ONE `i` variable in memory for the entire loop. When the loop finishes, `i` is 3. Later, when the `setTimeout` callbacks execute, they all look up that exact same `i` reference in the closure, which is now 3. `let`, on the other hand, is block-scoped, creating a brand new, distinct `i` variable in memory for every single iteration.
drills.spokenDefence: 'The classic `var` loop issue is a scoping problem. The callbacks close over a single shared variable binding. By changing `var` to `let`, we create a new lexical environment for each iteration, meaning each callback closes over a fresh, immutable copy of `i` for that specific loop step.'
acceptanceCriteria: Should log correct indices via closure capture (IIFE or setTimeout args).

mcq.q: Besides changing `var` to `let`, how else can you fix the `var` loop closure bug in legacy code?
options: Use an Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE) to capture the value.
Pass `i` as the third argument to `setTimeout`.
mcq.why: An IIFE creates a new function scope, capturing the current value of `i`. `setTimeout(fn, ms, arg1)` passes the arguments directly to the callback.

drills.title: Redux Data Flow & Purity
drills.hook: Why must Redux reducers be absolutely pure? What happens if you mutate state directly?
drills.deepDive: Redux uses shallow equality (`===`) to determine if the state has changed. If you mutate a nested array (e.g., `state.users.push(newUser)`) and return the same state object, the reference hasn't changed. React-Redux (`useSelector`) will see `oldState === newState`, assume nothing happened, and completely skip the re-render. Reducers must return a brand new object/array reference (`...state`) to break the equality check.
drills.spokenDefence: 'Reducers are pure functions mapping `(state, action) => newState`. If you mutate state, you destroy the immutability contract. Redux relies on strict reference equality checks for performance; mutating state means `useSelector` won't trigger a re-render. This is why tools like Redux Toolkit use Immer under the hood to let you write mutating syntax that compiles into immutable updates.'
acceptanceCriteria: Should return a completely new state tree branch immutably.

mcq.q: Which of the following reducer cases is valid and will trigger a UI update?
mcq.why: Option C creates a completely new root object reference without mutating the original state object. Object.assign into `state` mutates the original reference.

drills.title: React Router v6 Paradigms
drills.hook: How does React Router change the URL without causing a full page reload?
drills.deepDive: React Router uses the HTML5 History API (`pushState` and `replaceState`). When you click a `<Link>`, it intercepts the default `<a>` tag behavior (`e.preventDefault()`), pushes the new URL to the browser history, and updates a global context state. The `<Routes>` component listens to this context, unmounts the old component, and mounts the new one matching the path.
drills.spokenDefence: 'React Router bridges the browser's History API with React's component tree. In v6, nested routing is handled seamlessly with the `<Outlet>` component, acting as a placeholder for child routes. This allows for persistent UI elements like sidebars while only re-rendering the inner page content.'
acceptanceCriteria: Should correctly use Outlet and nested Routes.

mcq.q: In React Router v6, what is the purpose of the `<Outlet />` component?
options: It forces a hard reload of the page.
It acts as a placeholder to render nested child route components.
It defines the root router provider.
mcq.why: `<Outlet />` is placed in a parent route layout to tell React Router where to render the matching child routes.

drills.title: Webpack & Tree Shaking
drills.hook: How does Webpack know which code is 'dead' and can be safely deleted from your final production bundle?
drills.deepDive: This process is called 'Tree Shaking'. It relies entirely on the static nature of ES6 modules (`import`/`export`). Because ES6 modules are static, bundlers can analyze the dependency tree at compile-time (unlike `require()`, which is dynamic). If an exported function is never imported anywhere, Webpack marks it as dead code. The minifier (like Terser) then completely removes it from the final bundle.
drills.spokenDefence: 'Tree shaking is dead-code elimination. It only works with ES6 modules because their static structure allows the bundler to map dependencies without executing the code. To ensure it works, we must ensure Babel isn't transpiling our imports down to CommonJS (`require`), and we must be careful with 'side effects' (code that executes just by importing a file).'
acceptanceCriteria: Should use ES6 static imports/exports for tree-shaking support.

mcq.q: Why does Tree Shaking fail if you use CommonJS `require()`?
options: CommonJS modules are evaluated dynamically at runtime, so the bundler cannot prove what is used.
mcq.why: With `require()`, you can conditionally import modules inside `if` statements. The bundler cannot predict runtime paths, so it must bundle everything.

It is written explicitly here only so you can see the failure — in a real stylesheet the universal reset *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box } does it once for everything.

drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Replace both hardcoded values: hover → color-mix(in oklch,var(--brand) 85%,black), tint → color-mix(in oklch,var(--brand) 10%,var(--surface)).
drills.takeaway: Two colours from one token. Change --brand and every derived shade follows.

drills.title: STACK — the highest-leverage class in CSS
drills.hook: .stack > * + * is the owl selector: 'every child that has a sibling before it'. Margin is a property of the RELATIONSHIP between two elements, not of ...
drills.deepDive: .stack > * + * is the owl selector: 'every child that has a sibling before it'. Margin is a property of the RELATIONSHIP between two elements, not of an element. So no leftover margin on the last child, ever. One class replaces every margin-bottom you would have written.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add margin-block-start:var(--space,var(--m)). Then add style="--space:var(--xl)" to the .stack element and watch it re-space.
drills.takeaway: One class, all vertical rhythm. --space overrides per instance without a new class.

drills.title: CLUSTER and BETWEEN — everything horizontal
drills.hook: .cluster = flex + wrap + gap + align-center: any row of things that should wrap gracefully. .between adds space-between: the whole action-bar archetyp...
drills.deepDive: .cluster = flex + wrap + gap + align-center: any row of things that should wrap gracefully. .between adds space-between: the whole action-bar archetype.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: cluster → display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:var(--m);align-items:center. between → same plus justify-content:space-between. Then drag narrow.
drills.takeaway: cluster = a wrapping row. between = the same, pushed apart. Two classes, every toolbar you'll ever build.

drills.title: SIDEBAR — responsive with NO media query
drills.hook: The trick: the sidebar gets a fixed-ish basis; the main gets flex-grow:999 so it eats all spare space, plus min-inline-size:50%. When main would drop ...
drills.deepDive: The trick: the sidebar gets a fixed-ish basis; the main gets flex-grow:999 so it eats all spare space, plus min-inline-size:50%. When main would drop under 50%, flex-wrap fires and they stack. The layout responds to its OWN width, not the viewport's.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: first-child → add flex-grow:1. last-child → flex-basis:0; flex-grow:999; min-inline-size:50%. Then drag the preview's right edge.
drills.takeaway: flex-grow:999 + min-inline-size:50% = self-collapsing. Zero media queries. This is the disruptive one.

drills.title: SWITCHER — equal columns that stack themselves
drills.hook: flex-basis:calc((30rem - 100%) * 999). If the container is wider than 30rem the calc goes negative, clamps to 0, and items share equally. Narrower, it...
drills.deepDive: flex-basis:calc((30rem - 100%) * 999). If the container is wider than 30rem the calc goes negative, clamps to 0, and items share equally. Narrower, it goes huge, and each item takes a full line. One line of maths replaces a media query.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add flex-basis:calc((30rem - 100%) * 999). Drag the preview across ~480px.
drills.takeaway: The Holy Albatross. Container-relative switching, no media query, one line.

drills.title: EXCEPTIONS — data attributes, not modifier classes
drills.hook: BEM gives you .btn--primary, .btn--ghost, .btn--danger, .btn--primary-large… an explosion. CUBE uses a data attribute: one hook, readable in the DOM, ...
drills.deepDive: BEM gives you .btn--primary, .btn--ghost, .btn--danger, .btn--primary-large… an explosion. CUBE uses a data attribute: one hook, readable in the DOM, usable by JS too.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: ghost → background:none;border-color:transparent. danger → color:var(--danger);border-color:var(--danger).
drills.takeaway: One attribute hook per variation. data-tone works on ANY block — that is why it is not .btn--danger.

drills.title: Putting it together — the whole dashboard, no new CSS
drills.hook: Everything below is composed from classes you already wrote. Read the class attributes: that is where the layout now lives. Component CSS: zero lines....
drills.deepDive: Everything below is composed from classes you already wrote. Read the class attributes: that is where the layout now lives. Component CSS: zero lines.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Change nothing. Drag the preview from wide to narrow and watch three layouts respond independently. Then change --m to 1.5rem — the whole page re-spaces from one edit.
drills.takeaway: Five words carry it: stack · cluster · sidebar · switcher · center. That is the entire memory load.

drills.title: THE DECISION — Grid when the parent decides, Flex when the content decides
drills.hook: This is the rule the whole system hangs on, and it is the answer to "why Grid here and Flex there?" in an interview.Grid — you know the structure up f...
drills.deepDive: This is the rule the whole system hangs on, and it is the answer to "why Grid here and Flex there?" in an interview.Grid — you know the structure up front. Tracks, 2D, alignment across rows. The parent dictates sizing, top-down.Flex — you do not control the count or the widths. One direction, content-driven, should wrap on its own.The tell: if you are reaching for a third nested container to make things line up, you needed Grid one level higher.Core. This is the most likely CSS architecture question in the technical round, and the reasoning behind half the Mettl layout MCQs. Own it cold.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Change grid-template-columns to 1fr 2fr 1fr — the PARENT resized all three children. Now try to do that to the button row without touching the buttons. You cannot: that row is content-driven, which is why it is flex.
drills.takeaway: Grid = parent decides tracks, top-down, 2D. Flex = content decides, one direction, wraps. Ask 'who owns the sizing?' and the answer picks itself.

drills.title: Flat beats nested — the anti-pattern you are being hired to avoid
drills.hook: The old way to get a header, sidebar, main and footer was four or five nested flex containers, each one existing only to hold the next. It works, but ...
drills.deepDive: The old way to get a header, sidebar, main and footer was four or five nested flex containers, each one existing only to hold the next. It works, but the structure lies about the layout and every change means re-reading the whole nest.One grid with named areas replaces the entire nest. The markup goes flat, and the layout becomes readable as ASCII.Core. grid-template-areas is plain Grid — squarely inside Mettl's CSS3 scope, and the cleanest answer to "how would you build this dashboard?"
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Swap the sidebar to the right: change the areas to "hd hd" / "mn sb" / "ft ft" and the columns to 1fr 8rem. Four HTML elements, zero wrappers, one edit.
drills.takeaway: Named areas = flat markup + a layout you can read. Nesting containers to fake structure is the 2020 habit; this replaces it.

drills.title: BONUSSUBGRID — align card internals across cards, no fixed heights
drills.hook: Cards in a row never line up: one has a longer title, so its button sits lower. The old fixes were fixed heights or JS.Subgrid lets a child inherit th...
drills.deepDive: Cards in a row never line up: one has a longer title, so its button sits lower. The old fixes were fixed heights or JS.Subgrid lets a child inherit the PARENT's row tracks. Each card spans the same three rows, so every title, body and button aligns across the whole row — automatically, at any content length.Exam weighting: Mettl names Flexbox and responsive design in its CSS3 competency list — it does not name this. Understand what it solves so you can say one sentence about it in the technical round. Do not drill it.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Make the buttons line up: on .cards add grid-template-rows:auto auto auto; on .c add grid-row:span 3 and grid-template-rows:subgrid. The cards now share the parent's rows.
drills.takeaway: subgrid = the child adopts the parent's tracks. Cross-card alignment with no fixed heights, no JS, no nesting.

drills.title: BONUSCONTAINER QUERIES — a component that responds to ITSELF
drills.hook: A media query asks how wide the viewport is. That is the wrong question for a component that might sit in a wide main column or a narrow sidebar.conta...
drills.deepDive: A media query asks how wide the viewport is. That is the wrong question for a component that might sit in a wide main column or a narrow sidebar.container-type:inline-size turns a parent into a query container; @container then asks how wide that box is. This is what finally kills the old flexbox width hacks — a component becomes genuinely portable.Exam weighting: Mettl names Flexbox and responsive design in its CSS3 competency list — it does not name this. Understand what it solves so you can say one sentence about it in the technical round. Do not drill it.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add container-type:inline-size to .contains, then inside the @container block set .card{grid-template-columns:5rem 1fr;align-items:center}. One component, two layouts, and NOT a media query in sight.
drills.takeaway: container-type on the parent, @container on the child. The component responds to its own box — which is why it can be dropped anywhere.

drills.title: Space on one scale — not arbitrary numbers
drills.hook: The fastest way a UI looks amateur is spacing picked ad hoc: 13px here, 7px there. Pick one scale and only ever use values from it. Four steps is enou...
drills.deepDive: The fastest way a UI looks amateur is spacing picked ad hoc: 13px here, 7px there. Pick one scale and only ever use values from it. Four steps is enough: 8 / 16 / 24 / 32.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Four values, all snapped to the scale. Nothing else changed — and it already looks deliberate.

drills.title: Measure and line-height — text that reads
drills.hook: Two numbers do almost all typographic work. Measure: 60–75 characters per line (max-width:65ch). Line-height: ~1.5 body, ~1.2 headings. Over-long line...
drills.deepDive: Two numbers do almost all typographic work. Measure: 60–75 characters per line (max-width:65ch). Line-height: ~1.5 body, ~1.2 headings. Over-long lines are the most common readability failure on the web.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Two properties. The paragraph stops being a wall and starts being prose.

drills.title: Hierarchy by weight and colour — not by size
drills.hook: Beginners scale font-size for every level and end up with six sizes fighting. Professionals hold size nearly constant and vary weight and colour. Two ...
drills.deepDive: Beginners scale font-size for every level and end up with six sizes fighting. Professionals hold size nearly constant and vary weight and colour. Two sizes, three weights, two greys is a complete hierarchy.The left card is the control — everything at one size and weight. Change only the right card and watch the two diverge.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Give the right card a real hierarchy: eyebrow 12px/700/uppercase with letter-spacing:.08em and color:dimgray · h3 20px/600 · body 15px · meta 13px and color:darkgray. Same words, same markup — compare against the left.
drills.why: Same words, same markup. All the hierarchy now comes from weight, colour and letter-spacing.

drills.title: Two shadows, used as elevation
drills.hook: Not ten shadows — two. A small one for resting cards, a larger one for things that float (menus, modals). Low opacity, offset downward: light comes fr...
drills.deepDive: Not ten shadows — two. A small one for resting cards, a larger one for things that float (menus, modals). Low opacity, offset downward: light comes from above.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Two soft layers beat one heavy blur. A tight shadow for the edge, a wide one for the lift.

drills.title: Radius consistency — and the nesting rule
drills.hook: Pick one radius, use it everywhere. When a rounded thing sits inside another rounded thing the inner radius must be smaller or the corners fight. Rule...
drills.deepDive: Pick one radius, use it everywhere. When a rounded thing sits inside another rounded thing the inner radius must be smaller or the corners fight. Rule of thumb: inner = outer − padding.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: One number changed. The corners stop competing. Same rule for buttons inside cards.

drills.title: Borders: hairline, and tinted rather than grey
drills.hook: A 2px mid-grey border is louder than it needs to be. Go 1px and tint it — a translucent black sits on any background. The UI gets calmer without losin...
drills.deepDive: A 2px mid-grey border is louder than it needs to be. Go 1px and tint it — a translucent black sits on any background. The UI gets calmer without losing structure.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Half the weight, a tenth the noise. Often you can drop the border entirely and let a shadow do the work.

drills.title: Transitions — 150ms, on interactive things only
drills.hook: Motion signals 'this responds to you'. Keep it short (120–200ms), and put it ONLY on interactive elements. Never transition all — name the properties ...
drills.deepDive: Motion signals 'this responds to you'. Keep it short (120–200ms), and put it ONLY on interactive elements. Never transition all — name the properties you mean.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: One line. Hover both buttons before and after — the difference is the whole feel of the control.

drills.title: Affordance — hover, active, focus, accent-color
drills.hook: Three states make a control feel real: hover (shift the colour), active (nudge 1px down), focus-visible (a ring). And accent-color themes native check...
drills.deepDive: Three states make a control feel real: hover (shift the colour), active (nudge 1px down), focus-visible (a ring). And accent-color themes native checkboxes and radios in a single line.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Click into the preview and press Tab. Four rules and the control finally feels like a control.

drills.title: Respect the user — reduced motion and colour-scheme
drills.hook: Two rules that cost nothing and mark you as someone who ships real products. prefers-reduced-motion honours people who get sick from animation. color-...
drills.deepDive: Two rules that cost nothing and mark you as someone who ships real products. prefers-reduced-motion honours people who get sick from animation. color-scheme makes native controls and scrollbars match your theme.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Two rules, zero visual cost in the default case, and a real difference for people who need them.

drills.title: Why rem exists — it is an accessibility feature, not a style choice
drills.hook: rem = root em = relative to the <html> font-size, which defaults to 16px. When a user raises their browser's default font size — and a lot of pe...
drills.deepDive: rem = root em = relative to the <html> font-size, which defaults to 16px. When a user raises their browser's default font size — and a lot of people do — everything in rem scales and everything in px ignores them. That is the whole argument. It is not aesthetics.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: The container is simulating a 20px root. Flip the toggle: the px version stays stubbornly small; the rem version respects the user.

drills.title: The rem scale you memorise once
drills.hook: At the default 16px root the maths is clean, and it lands exactly on the 8/16/24/32 spacing scale you already know. Learn these seven and you never co...
drills.deepDive: At the default 16px root the maths is clean, and it lands exactly on the 8/16/24/32 spacing scale you already know. Learn these seven and you never convert again:.25rem=4 · .5rem=8 · .75rem=12 · 1rem=16 · 1.5rem=24 · 2rem=32 · 3rem=48
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Identical rendering at the default root — but only one version survives a user who changes their font size. Same pixels today, different behaviour tomorrow.

drills.title: em — relative to THIS element, and it compounds
drills.hook: em is relative to the current element's font-size, so it multiplies when nested — that is the footgun. But it is also exactly what you want for paddin...
drills.deepDive: em is relative to the current element's font-size, so it multiplies when nested — that is the footgun. But it is also exactly what you want for padding inside a control: padding:.5em 1em makes a button's padding scale with its own text, so one rule works for small and large buttons.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: One rule, three sizes. With px all three get identical padding and the large button looks cramped; with em the padding follows the text.

drills.title: Where px still wins — do not cargo-cult
drills.hook: "Never use px" is folklore. Some things should not scale with text: hairline borders, shadow offsets and blurs, and 1px dividers. A 1px border in rem ...
drills.deepDive: "Never use px" is folklore. Some things should not scale with text: hairline borders, shadow offsets and blurs, and 1px dividers. A 1px border in rem becomes 2px at large font settings and the UI looks heavier for no reason. Rule: type and space in rem, hairlines and shadows in px.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Both look identical here. The px version stays a true hairline at any zoom level; the rem version thickens. Keep hairlines in px on purpose, and be able to say why.

drills.title: Viewport units — and the two traps
drills.hook: vh/vw are 1% of the viewport. Two traps: (1) 100vh is wrong on mobile — it ignores the browser chrome, so content hides behind it. Use 100dvh (dynamic...
drills.deepDive: vh/vw are 1% of the viewport. Two traps: (1) 100vh is wrong on mobile — it ignores the browser chrome, so content hides behind it. Use 100dvh (dynamic). (2) width:100vw includes the scrollbar and causes horizontal overflow. Use 100%, or inset:0 for overlays.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Same result on desktop. On a phone the first version puts content under the URL bar and produces a sideways scroll. Two characters of difference.

drills.title: clamp() — fluid type, no media query, zoom still works
drills.hook: clamp(min, preferred, max). Put a rem floor and a rem ceiling around a vw middle and you get type that scales with the viewport but never gets unreada...
drills.deepDive: clamp(min, preferred, max). Put a rem floor and a rem ceiling around a vw middle and you get type that scales with the viewport but never gets unreadably small or absurdly large.Never size text in raw vw. It makes browser zoom do nothing — a genuine accessibility failure.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: Drag the preview. Raw vw keeps shrinking past readable and kills zoom; clamp holds a floor and a ceiling. The `1rem +` part keeps it zoom-responsive.

drills.title: Breakpoints and measure — em and ch
drills.hook: Two more relative units earn their place. Media queries in em (not px) so breakpoints respect the user's font size — @media (min-width:40em) = 640px a...
drills.deepDive: Two more relative units earn their place. Media queries in em (not px) so breakpoints respect the user's font size — @media (min-width:40em) = 640px at default. And ch for line length: max-width:65ch is literally "65 characters wide", which is the readability target.The top card has no measure — full width, however wide the pane is. Yours is below it.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: ch says what you mean. em breakpoints move with the user's font size — px breakpoints do not.

drills.title: The whole rule, on one line
drills.hook: Type and space in rem. Component-internal padding in em. Line length in ch. Full-height in dvh. Fluid type in clamp() with rem bounds. Hairlines and s...
drills.deepDive: Type and space in rem. Component-internal padding in em. Line length in ch. Full-height in dvh. Fluid type in clamp() with rem bounds. Hairlines and shadows stay px.That is the entire unit system. Everything below is that sentence applied.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Follows architecture guidelines.
drills.why: One component, every rule applied. Note the border stayed px on purpose — that is the part most people get wrong in the other direction.

drills.title: Centred card — cover + box
drills.hook: Two classes. cover centres on both axes; box is the card. The old version needed six declarations....
drills.deepDive: Two classes. cover centres on both axes; box is the card. The old version needed six declarations.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Delete cover from the outer div — it drops to the top-left. Put it back.
drills.takeaway: cover = centred. box = card. stack = rhythm inside. Zero new CSS.

drills.title: Action bar — between + cluster
drills.hook: between pushes the two halves apart and wraps; cluster keeps the buttons together. That is the whole toolbar....
drills.deepDive: between pushes the two halves apart and wraps; cluster keeps the buttons together. That is the whole toolbar.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Drag the preview narrow — it wraps on its own. Then swap between for cluster and see the difference.
drills.takeaway: between = pushed apart. cluster = held together. Both wrap by default.

drills.title: App shell — sidebar, and no media query
drills.hook: The old version needed grid-template-areas plus a breakpoint. sidebar collapses on its own, based on its own width rather than the viewport's....
drills.deepDive: The old version needed grid-template-areas plus a breakpoint. sidebar collapses on its own, based on its own width rather than the viewport's.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add style="--side:8rem" to the .sidebar div — the fixed side narrows without touching CSS.
drills.takeaway: sidebar = self-collapsing two-column. --side tunes it per instance.

drills.title: Card grid — grid-auto
drills.hook: One class. --col tunes the minimum column width per instance, so you never write a second grid rule....
drills.deepDive: One class. --col tunes the minimum column width per instance, so you never write a second grid rule.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add style="--col:8rem" to the grid — more, narrower columns. Then --col:20rem.
drills.takeaway: grid-auto = responsive cards, one class, tuned by --col.

drills.title: Equal columns — switcher
drills.hook: Pricing tables, feature triplets, stat rows. All children stay equal until the container is too narrow, then each takes a full line....
drills.deepDive: Pricing tables, feature triplets, stat rows. All children stay equal until the container is too narrow, then each takes a full line.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add style="--threshold:16rem" to the switcher and drag — it now switches at a different width.
drills.takeaway: switcher = equal-or-stacked, container-relative, one line of maths, no breakpoint.

drills.title: The whole screen — every primitive at once
drills.hook: Read the class attributes top to bottom. That is where the layout lives now; the CSS pane below is empty on purpose....
drills.deepDive: Read the class attributes top to bottom. That is where the layout lives now; the CSS pane below is empty on purpose.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add :root{--m:1.5rem} and watch the whole page re-space from one edit.
drills.takeaway: Five words carried an entire dashboard: stack · cluster · between · sidebar · grid-auto.

drills.title: JSX is not HTML — it is JavaScript that returns elements
drills.hook: Everything inside return ( … ) is compiled to function calls. That is why it obeys JS rules, not HTML rules: one root element, every tag closed, and {...
drills.deepDive: Everything inside return ( … ) is compiled to function calls. That is why it obeys JS rules, not HTML rules: one root element, every tag closed, and { } drops you back into JavaScript.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Delete the wrapping <div> so there are two roots. Read the error — 'must have one parent element'. Then put it back.
drills.takeaway: One root. Every tag closed. { } is an escape hatch back into JavaScript.

drills.title: className, not class — and why
drills.hook: class is a reserved word in JavaScript, so JSX uses className. Same for for → htmlFor. Everything else (id, data-*, aria-*) keeps its HTML name exactl...
drills.deepDive: class is a reserved word in JavaScript, so JSX uses className. Same for for → htmlFor. Everything else (id, data-*, aria-*) keeps its HTML name exactly.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Change className to class and watch the styling break. Note the self-closing <input /> — JSX requires the slash.
drills.takeaway:
className and htmlFor are the only two renames. Void elements MUST self-close: , ,
.

drills.title: Composing classes — this is where your layout lives
drills.hook: You already own these. In JSX they go in className, space-separated, and they compose: "box stack" means a bordered card whose children are vertically...
drills.deepDive: You already own these. In JSX they go in className, space-separated, and they compose: "box stack" means a bordered card whose children are vertically spaced.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Read each className aloud: stack = vertical rhythm · between = pushed apart · box = card · sidebar = self-collapsing two-column · grid-auto = responsive cards. Now drag the preview narrow.
drills.takeaway: stack · cluster · between · sidebar · switcher · center · grid-auto · box. Layout lives in className, not in new CSS.

drills.title: style={{ }} — the double brace, explained
drills.hook: The outer { } means 'JavaScript here'. The inner { } is an object literal. So it is not special syntax — it is an object inside an expression slot. Pr...
drills.deepDive: The outer { } means 'JavaScript here'. The inner { } is an object literal. So it is not special syntax — it is an object inside an expression slot. Properties are camelCase and numbers are treated as px.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add borderLeft: '.25rem solid steelblue' to the outer div. Then try background-color and see it silently do nothing.

drills.title: .map() — rendering a list
drills.hook: A list is an array transformed into elements. { } to enter JS, .map() to transform, and each item needs a stable key — the identity React uses to matc...
drills.deepDive: A list is an array transformed into elements. { } to enter JS, .map() to transform, and each item needs a stable key — the identity React uses to match elements across renders. Never the array index for a list that can reorder or delete.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add a fourth person. Then change key={p.id} to key={i} (add , i to the map params) — it still renders, which is exactly why the bug is so easy to ship.

drills.hook: Everything here is composed from classes you already have. Read it as: shell → bar → sidebar → grid → list. That is the whole job....
