drills.title: useState — the whole model in four lines
drills.hook: const [value, setValue] = useState(initial). Calling setValue does two things: it stores the new value and asks React to run your component again. The...
drills.deepDive: const [value, setValue] = useState(initial). Calling setValue does two things: it stores the new value and asks React to run your component again. The screen is a function of state — you never touch the DOM.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Add a Reset button that calls setCount(0). Then try changing count directly with count = 5 — nothing happens, because that does not tell React to re-render.
drills.takeaway: State = memory + a re-render request. Never mutate state directly; always call the setter.

drills.title: The functional updater — and why two clicks can equal one
drills.hook: setCount(count + 1) reads count from this render's closure. Call it twice in one handler and both read the same stale value, so you get +1 not +2. set...
drills.deepDive: setCount(count + 1) reads count from this render's closure. Call it twice in one handler and both read the same stale value, so you get +1 not +2. setCount(c => c + 1) receives the latest value instead.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Click each button and watch the difference. This exact snippet is a top-5 MCQ trap and a real production bug.
drills.takeaway: Two setState calls that read the current value both see the SAME value. Use the updater form whenever the next value depends on the previous one.

drills.title: Controlled inputs — the value comes from state
drills.hook: A controlled input has value={state} and onChange writing back. React owns the value; the DOM just displays it. That is why you can transform, validat...
drills.deepDive: A controlled input has value={state} and onChange writing back. React owns the value; the DOM just displays it. That is why you can transform, validate or block input on the way through.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Make it uppercase on the way in: setName(e.target.value.toUpperCase()). Then remove onChange entirely — the input freezes, because state never changes.
drills.takeaway: value + onChange = controlled. Remove onChange and the field becomes read-only — a classic 'why can't I type' bug.

drills.title: Derived state — compute during render, never store it
drills.hook: If a value can be calculated from existing state, calculate it. Storing it in a second useState means two sources of truth that drift apart. This is t...
drills.deepDive: If a value can be calculated from existing state, calculate it. Storing it in a second useState means two sources of truth that drift apart. This is the single most common architecture mistake in React.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Note there is no useState for shown or remaining. Try adding one and keeping it in sync — you will feel why it is a trap.
drills.takeaway: Derive, do not store. Two useStates that must agree will eventually disagree.

drills.title: Updating arrays immutably — add, remove, toggle
drills.hook: React compares by reference. Mutating an array with push keeps the same reference, so React sees no change and skips the re-render. Always produce a n...
drills.deepDive: React compares by reference. Mutating an array with push keeps the same reference, so React sees no change and skips the re-render. Always produce a new array.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Replace setTodos([...todos, …]) with todos.push(…); setTodos(todos) — the item is added to the array but the screen never updates. That is the reference bug, live.
drills.takeaway: add = [...xs, n] · remove = xs.filter() · toggle = xs.map(). Three lines cover every list CRUD you will be asked for.

drills.title: useEffect — for things outside React, with cleanup
drills.hook: Effects are for the outside world: timers, subscriptions, network. The return is the cleanup and it runs before the next effect and on unmount. A time...
drills.deepDive: Effects are for the outside world: timers, subscriptions, network. The return is the cleanup and it runs before the next effect and on unmount. A timer without cleanup is a memory leak and a doubled interval.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Delete the return () => clearInterval(id) line, then start and stop a few times — the counter accelerates because old intervals never died.
drills.takeaway: Every subscription needs a cleanup. Note setSecs(s => s+1) — without the updater this would freeze at 1 (stale closure).

drills.title: Lifting state — two components, one source of truth
drills.hook: When two parts of the UI need the same value, the state moves up to their closest common parent and comes back down as props. Callbacks go down too, s...
drills.deepDive: When two parts of the UI need the same value, the state moves up to their closest common parent and comes back down as props. Callbacks go down too, so children can ask the parent to change it.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: The Chip has no state at all — it receives active and calls onPick. Add a fourth tab and it just works.
drills.takeaway: State up, props down, callbacks up. Dumb children, one owner. This is the answer to 'how do you share state?'

drills.title: A complete feature — everything at once
drills.hook: Search + filter + add + toggle + delete + empty state + count. This is a Tier-S machine-coding task, fully functional, in one screen....
drills.deepDive: Search + filter + add + toggle + delete + empty state + count. This is a Tier-S machine-coding task, fully functional, in one screen.
drills.spokenDefence: "This pattern ensures clear separation of concerns, making the component easier to test and highly predictable across renders."
acceptanceCriteria: Everything works. Now count the state: four useState calls, zero derived values stored. That ratio is what an interviewer is reading.
drills.takeaway: Minimal state, everything else derived. Four hooks carried a full CRUD feature with search, filters and an empty state.

drills.title: The Infinite Loop Trap (useEffect)
drills.hook: Updating state inside a useEffect without dependencies causes an infinite render loop.
drills.deepDive: When a component renders, the useEffect runs. If it calls a state setter, the component re-renders. If the dependency array is missing, the effect runs AFTER EVERY render, immediately setting state again and triggering another render. This will crash the browser tab.
drills.spokenDefence: "If an interviewer shows me a component crashing the tab, the first thing I look for is an unconditional state update inside the render body, or a useEffect missing a dependency array. By adding the empty array [], we instruct React to only run the effect once after the initial mount, acting like componentDidMount."
acceptanceCriteria: Identifies the missing dependency array.
Prevents the infinite render loop.

mcq.q: What is the difference between useEffect with [] vs no array at all?
options: [] runs once. No array runs after every render.
No array runs only on mount.
mcq.why: No array means "run after every render". [] means "run when dependencies change", and since it has none, it runs only once.

drills.title: Context API Re-render Waterfall
drills.hook: Passing a new object reference to a Context Provider value causes ALL consumers to re-render, even if the data inside hasn't changed.
drills.deepDive: When the parent of a Context.Provider re-renders, it evaluates `value={{ user, theme }}`. This creates a brand new object in memory (a new pointer). React compares the old value to the new value using `Object.is()`. Since the pointers are different, it forces a re-render of every component consuming that context. You must wrap the object in `useMemo` to preserve referential equality.
drills.spokenDefence: "In technical rounds, if asked how to optimize Context API, I explain referential equality. I always wrap the Provider's value object in useMemo. Otherwise, any unrelated state change in the parent creates a new object reference, triggering a catastrophic re-render waterfall for every consumer down the tree."
acceptanceCriteria: Identifies the inline object recreation.
Uses useMemo to cache the context value.

mcq.q: How do you prevent a Context Provider from creating a new object reference on every render?
mcq.why: useMemo caches the object reference between renders unless its dependencies change.

drills.title: Building useDebounce (Mettl OA Classic)
drills.hook: Debouncing delays a state update until a certain amount of time has passed without any new updates.
drills.deepDive: In a search bar, typing "React" triggers 5 state updates. If you fetch data on every keystroke, you DDoS your own backend. `useDebounce` is a custom hook that takes a value and a delay. It sets a timeout to update a `debouncedValue` state. If the value changes before the timeout finishes, the `useEffect` cleanup function clears the previous timeout, preventing the update.
drills.spokenDefence: "Writing a useDebounce hook is my go-to signal for senior-level React knowledge. It perfectly demonstrates understanding of useEffect cleanup functions. By clearing the timeout in the cleanup phase, we guarantee that only the final keystroke (after the user pauses) actually triggers the debounced state update."
acceptanceCriteria: Implements setTimeout inside useEffect.
Implements clearTimeout in the cleanup return function.

mcq.q: When does the useEffect cleanup function run?
options: Before the effect runs again, and on unmount.
mcq.why: React runs the cleanup function to clean up the previous render's effect BEFORE running the new effect.

drills.title: React.memo & The Inline Prop Trap
drills.hook: React.memo prevents re-renders, but passing an inline array `[]` or function `() => {}` instantly breaks it.
drills.deepDive: When a parent renders, it creates new memory pointers for any inline arrays, objects, or functions. If you pass `data={[1,2,3]}` to a child wrapped in `React.memo`, the memoization fails because `[1,2,3] !== [1,2,3]` in memory. You must wrap the prop in `useMemo` or move it outside the component if it's static.
drills.spokenDefence: "A classic optimization mistake is wrapping a component in React.memo but passing it an inline function or array. In interviews, I point out that React.memo does a shallow comparison (===). I always cache the prop with useMemo or useCallback before passing it down, ensuring referential equality and successfully blocking the re-render waterfall."
acceptanceCriteria: Identifies the inline array breaking memoization.
Implements useMemo to stabilize the array reference.

mcq.q: Which prop will BREAK React.memo on a child component?
mcq.why: An inline function creates a new pointer on every render, failing the shallow comparison.

drills.title: Stale Closures in Event Listeners
drills.hook: An event listener attached inside `useEffect` with `[]` captures the state variables of the FIRST render forever.
drills.deepDive: If you do `window.addEventListener("scroll", handleScroll)` inside a mount-only useEffect, the `handleScroll` function is a closure from the first render. If it tries to read `count`, it will always see `0`. To fix this, you must either include the state in the dependency array (which forces re-attachment of the listener), or use a mutable `useRef` to store the latest state.
drills.spokenDefence: "When attaching global event listeners or websockets, stale closures are the #1 source of bugs. If the listener reads state, I either use the functional update pattern `setCount(c => c + 1)`, or I synchronize the latest state into a `useRef` so the stale closure can read `ref.current` and get fresh data without needing to re-attach the listener constantly."
acceptanceCriteria: Understands the stale closure trap.
Implements useRef to bypass the closure and read fresh state.

mcq.q: How does `useRef` solve the stale closure problem in an event listener?
options: It forces the listener to re-attach.
Its .current property is mutable and shares the same memory address across all renders.
mcq.why: Because the ref object is mutated rather than recreated, the closure holding the ref pointer can read the updated .current value at any time.

drills.title: useReducer for Complex State Transitions
drills.hook: When multiple state variables must change together in response to one action, `useState` creates race conditions. `useReducer` guarantees atomicity.
drills.deepDive: If clicking "Fetch" requires `setLoading(true)`, `setError(null)`, and `setData([])` simultaneously, doing them as 3 `useState` calls is brittle. `useReducer` allows you to dispatch a single `{ type: 'FETCH_START' }` action, letting the reducer predictably transition the state machine as a single atomic unit.
drills.spokenDefence: "For simple toggles, I use useState. But the moment state becomes a state machine—like a data fetching flow with idle, loading, success, and error states—I switch to useReducer. It centralizes the transition logic out of the component body, makes it easily unit-testable without rendering, and ensures impossible states (like having both data AND an error) cannot exist."
acceptanceCriteria: Implements FETCH_START (loading true, clear others).
Implements FETCH_SUCCESS (loading false, set data).
Implements FETCH_ERROR (loading false, set error).

mcq.q: What makes useReducer easier to test than useState?
options: Reducers are pure functions independent of React context.
mcq.why: A reducer takes (state, action) and returns a new state. It is a pure JavaScript function that can be imported into a Jest file and tested without rendering any components.

drills.title: The Searchable Data Grid
drills.hook: A data grid filtering locally requires derived state: you store the raw data, store the search query, and calculate the visible rows on the fly.
drills.deepDive: Never store "filteredData" in its own useState if it can be calculated from "allData" and "searchQuery". Syncing two states manually leads to bugs (e.g., when raw data updates but you forget to update the filtered array). Instead, derive it during render: `const visible = data.filter(d => d.name.includes(search))`.
drills.spokenDefence: "In machine coding rounds, a searchable list is the most common task. Interviewers look for two things: 1) Are you duplicating state (storing filtered results in useState), and 2) Are you using semantic HTML like tables or clean CSS grid? I always use derived state to ensure a single source of truth, and wrap the filtering logic in useMemo if the dataset is massive."
acceptanceCriteria: Maintains a single state for the search query.
Derives the filtered list dynamically during render.
Handles case-insensitive matching.

mcq.q: Why shouldn't you store `filteredUsers` in its own `useState`?
options: It creates redundant state that easily goes out of sync with the raw data.
useState can only hold strings and numbers.
mcq.why: Derived state (calculating the filtered list during render) guarantees that the UI always perfectly matches the raw data and search query.

drills.title: Interactive Star Rating
drills.hook: A 5-star rating component requires tracking two separate concepts: the permanently committed rating (onClick) and the temporary visual rating (onMouseEnter/Leave).
drills.deepDive: When hovering over star #4, stars 1-4 should light up, temporarily overriding the committed rating (say, 2). When the mouse leaves the widget entirely, it must snap back to the committed rating (2). This requires two states: `rating` and `hoverValue`.
drills.spokenDefence: "The star rating is a classic test of separating temporary visual state from committed data state. I structure it using an array mapped to indexes, passing the index to mouse handlers. I ensure the UI derives its active class by checking if the star's index is less than or equal to (hoverValue || rating)."
acceptanceCriteria: Maintains committed rating state.
Maintains temporary hover state.
Derives star appearance from (hover || rating).
Clears hover state onMouseLeave of the container.

mcq.q: What is the most robust way to generate 5 stars in React without hardcoding 5 elements?
options: A for loop pushing to an array.
mcq.why: Array(5).fill(0).map((_, i) => ...) is the standard, declarative React pattern for generating a fixed number of elements.

drills.title: Recursive Folder Tree
drills.hook: When data is infinitely nested (like a file system), you cannot hardcode the UI layers. A component must render ITSELF.
drills.deepDive: Recursive components are the only way to render arbitrary tree data. A `Folder` component takes a `node` prop. If the node has `children`, it renders its own title, and then maps over its children, returning `<Folder key={child.id} node={child} />` for each one. State for "isExpanded" lives inside the Folder component itself, so each level manages its own toggle.
drills.spokenDefence: "Recursive rendering is a frequent technical screen for Senior roles. It proves you understand component encapsulation. The trick is ensuring the recursion has a base case (e.g. no children means it's a file) and giving each instance its own local state for expanding/collapsing, rather than trying to track the open state of every node in a massive global Redux store."
acceptanceCriteria: Component renders itself recursively for children.
Uses local state for expand/collapse.
Properly distinguishes files vs folders (base case).

mcq.q: Where should the `isOpen` state live in a recursive tree?
options: In the top-level parent App component.
Inside the recursive Component itself, locally.
It shouldn't be state, it should be in the DOM.
mcq.why: Keeping isOpen local to the recursive component means you don't have to manage a complex dictionary of IDs and booleans in the parent.

drills.title: The Unbreakable Stopwatch
drills.hook: To build a stopwatch, you need a way to store the interval ID so you can clear it later. `useState` would cause a re-render just for saving the ID. `useRef` is the correct tool.
drills.deepDive: A ref is essentially a mutable object `{ current: initialValue }` that React guarantees will persist across re-renders. When you start an interval, you store the ID in `intervalRef.current = setInterval(...)`. This doesn't trigger a render. When you pause, you call `clearInterval(intervalRef.current)`.
drills.spokenDefence: "A common pitfall in stopwatch challenges is storing the timer ID in useState. This triggers an unnecessary render when starting the timer, and worse, if you try to clear it inside an unmount cleanup function, a stale closure might prevent you from accessing the correct ID. Storing the ID in a useRef ensures synchronous, stable access without polluting the render cycle."
acceptanceCriteria: Uses useRef to store the timer ID without triggering re-renders.
Prevents multiple simultaneous intervals on rapid clicking.
Clears the interval on unmount to prevent memory leaks.

mcq.q: Why is `useRef` preferred over `let timerId` declared outside the component?
options: A global let variable would be shared across ALL instances of the component, breaking if you render two stopwatches.
mcq.why: Variables outside a component are global to the module. If you render <Stopwatch /> twice, they will overwrite each other's timer IDs. useRef is scoped to the specific component instance.

mcqs.question: What is the output of this code?
mcqs.explanation: Object keys are stringified. Both `b` and `c` are objects, so they stringify to `"[object Object]"`. `a["[object Object]"]` is first set to 123, then overwritten with 456.

mcqs.code: console.log(typeof typeof 1);
mcqs.explanation: `typeof 1` returns the string `"number"`. Then `typeof "number"` returns the string `"string"`.

mcqs.question: What is the evaluation of this map function?
mcqs.explanation: `parseInt` takes two arguments: string and radix. `map` passes (element, index). So it runs: parseInt("1", 0) -> 1, parseInt("7", 1) -> NaN, parseInt("11", 2) -> 3.

mcqs.question: What gets logged to the console?
mcqs.explanation: `var` is function scoped. By the time the `setTimeout` callbacks run, the loop has completed and `i` is 3. All three callbacks reference the same `i`.

mcqs.question: What is the exact output order?
mcqs.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Microtasks (Promises) run next (3). Macrotasks (setTimeout) run last (2).

mcqs.question: What does this output?
mcqs.explanation: Regular functions bind `this` to the object calling it (shape). Arrow functions lexically bind `this` to the surrounding scope (window/global), where `radius` is undefined, resulting in NaN.

mcqs.question: What is the value of `count` on the screen after the button is clicked ONCE?
mcqs.explanation: React batches state updates. All three calls use the same captured closure value of `count` (0). So it runs `setCount(0+1)` three times. The result is 1.

mcqs.question: When will the `useEffect` cleanup function run in this component?
options: Before the component unmounts AND before the effect re-runs when `userId` changes.
After the new effect runs when `userId` changes.
mcqs.explanation: Cleanup functions run when the component unmounts, AND they run to clean up the previous effect *before* executing the new effect if the dependencies (`userId`) change.

mcqs.question: What happens if you mutate a state array directly instead of copying it?
options: The array updates and the component re-renders.
The array updates in memory, but the component DOES NOT re-render.
mcqs.explanation: React uses `Object.is` (reference equality) to check for state changes. Since the `items` array reference is exactly the same, React bails out and does not trigger a re-render.

mcqs.question: Why does React require a `key` prop when rendering a list of elements?
mcqs.code:
items.map(item =>
  • {item.name}
    • )
options: To help the React Reconciler identify which items have changed, are added, or are removed.
To pass data to the child component automatically.
mcqs.explanation: Keys give React elements a stable identity across renders, allowing the reconciliation algorithm (diffing) to efficiently update the DOM rather than destroying and recreating nodes.

mcqs.question: What is the primary difference between `useMemo` and `React.memo`?
mcqs.code: // Concept Question
options: `useMemo` memoizes a component, `React.memo` memoizes a value.
`useMemo` memoizes a calculated value inside a component, `React.memo` is a HOC that memoizes a whole component based on props.
They are aliases for the exact same function.
`useMemo` runs on the server, `React.memo` runs on the client.
mcqs.explanation: `useMemo` caches the result of an expensive calculation between renders. `React.memo` prevents a child component from re-rendering if its props have not changed.

mcqs.question: What does this log?
mcqs.explanation: Arrow functions have no own `this` — they close over the enclosing lexical scope, which here is the module/global, not `obj`. A shorthand method gets `this` from the call site, so `obj.greet2()` sees `obj`. Rule: never use an arrow for an object method that needs `this`.

mcqs.question: What is `b`?
mcqs.explanation: Defaults in destructuring apply only when the value is `undefined`. `a` is `{}`, so the `= {}` default is skipped; `b` is missing from it, so `b` takes its default of 5. Rule: destructuring defaults fire on `undefined`, never on `null` or `0`.

mcqs.question: How do you swap two variables in one line with destructuring?
mcqs.code: let a = 1, b = 2;
mcqs.explanation: Array destructuring evaluates the right-hand side first, then assigns positionally. Object destructuring cannot swap because the keys, not the positions, do the binding.

mcqs.question: A tagged template `tag`x${1}y`` receives which first argument?
options: An array of the string chunks: `["x", "y"]`
mcqs.explanation: A tag function receives the array of literal chunks first (with a `.raw` property), then each interpolated value as a separate argument. This is how libraries like styled-components read the CSS you write.

mcqs.question: Which statement about ES modules is TRUE?
options: Imports are hoisted and bindings are live — reassigning the export updates the importer
Imports are copies, so later changes in the module are invisible
`import` can be used conditionally inside an `if` block
ES modules execute in non-strict mode by default
mcqs.explanation: ES module bindings are live views, not copies; the importer sees a later reassignment. Static `import` is hoisted and cannot be conditional — that is what dynamic `import()` is for. Modules are always strict mode.

mcqs.question: What happens?
mcqs.explanation: Private class fields (`#count`) are only accessible inside the class body. Touching `a.#count` from outside is a **syntax** error, caught at parse time — not a runtime `undefined`.

mcqs.question: What does `[...new Set([1, 2, 2, 3])]` produce?
mcqs.explanation: A `Set` stores unique values by SameValueZero; spreading it back into an array is the idiomatic dedupe. Note `NaN` is considered equal to itself here, unlike `===`.

mcqs.question: What does this log?
mcqs.explanation: `this.constructor` on a `Child` instance is `Child`, and static methods are inherited through the prototype chain — so the override wins. Static inheritance is real inheritance, not a copy.

mcqs.question: What is the count after clicking once?
mcqs.explanation: `count` is captured by the closure at render time, so all three calls compute `0 + 1`. Rule: to build on the previous value use the functional updater — `setCount(c => c + 1)` — which would give 3.

mcqs.question: What does React actually do with the virtual DOM?
options: Diffs the new tree against the previous one and applies the minimal set of real DOM mutations
Renders the whole tree to the real DOM on every state change, and the browser deduplicates it
Keeps a copy of the real DOM in memory to read layout values faster
Replaces the browser DOM entirely with its own rendering engine
mcqs.explanation: The virtual DOM is a plain-object description of the UI. Reconciliation diffs old against new and commits only the differences. It is not faster than a hand-written minimal DOM update — it is faster than naive full re-rendering, and far easier to write.

mcqs.question: Which class lifecycle method is the correct place to fire a network request after the component first appears?
mcqs.explanation: `componentDidMount` runs once after the first commit, when the DOM exists and it is safe to `setState`. `componentWillMount` is deprecated, `render` must stay pure, and the constructor runs before mounting.

mcqs.question: What does `shouldComponentUpdate` returning `false` do?
options: Skips re-rendering this component and its children for that update
Skips this component but still re-renders its children
Cancels the state update entirely so state does not change
mcqs.explanation: It skips the render phase for that subtree; the state still changes. `React.PureComponent` implements it as a shallow prop/state comparison — the class equivalent of `React.memo`.

mcqs.question: A Higher Order Component is best described as:
options: A function that takes a component and returns a new component
A component that renders other components as children
A component defined at the top of the file
A hook that wraps another hook
mcqs.explanation: `withRouter`, `connect` and `withTheme` are HOCs: `Component => Component`. They compose behaviour without inheritance. Hooks largely replaced them, but Mettl lists HOCs as a named React competency.

mcqs.question: Which statement about props is TRUE?
options: Props are read-only — a component must never mutate its own props
Props can be mutated as long as you call `forceUpdate` afterwards
Props are copied deeply on every render
Props and state are the same thing with different names
mcqs.explanation: React components must behave like pure functions with respect to their props. Mutating props breaks the data flow the parent owns, and React will not re-render from it.

mcqs.question: A list is rendered with `key={index}` and a new item is inserted at the front. What goes wrong?
options: Every item after the insertion is treated as changed, so state inside those rows is attached to the wrong data
Nothing — index keys are equivalent to id keys
mcqs.explanation: Keys identify an element across renders. With index keys, inserting at the front shifts every index, so React matches row 0 to the new item and carries the old row state along with it. Rule: keys must be stable, unique and tied to the data.

mcqs.question: Why must you not mutate state directly, e.g. `state.items.push(x)`?
options: React compares by reference — the same array reference means no re-render
It throws a runtime error in production
Arrays cannot be mutated in JavaScript
It only breaks in class components
mcqs.explanation: React (and `memo`, and `PureComponent`) compares old and new values by reference. Mutating in place leaves the reference identical, so the update is invisible. Rule: replace, never mutate — `setItems([...items, x])`.

mcqs.question: What renders?
mcqs.explanation: `0 && x` short-circuits to `0`, and React renders the number 0 as text. `false`, `null` and `undefined` render nothing — `0` does not. Rule: guard with `items.length > 0 &&`.

mcqs.question: A `React.memo` component still re-renders on every parent render. The most likely cause is:
options: A prop is a new object/array/function literal created during the parent render
mcqs.explanation: `memo` does a shallow comparison. `<Child style={{a:1}} onX={() => …} />` creates fresh references every render, so the comparison always fails. Stabilise with `useMemo`/`useCallback` or hoist the literal.

mcqs.question: In React 18+ StrictMode (development), what happens to a component on mount?
options: It mounts, unmounts and remounts — effects run, clean up, then run again
It mounts once, exactly as in production
mcqs.explanation: StrictMode double-invokes render and re-runs effects in development to surface missing cleanup. It is a bug detector, not a bug: an effect that breaks under it is an effect with no cleanup.

mcqs.question: What does `props.children` contain?
options: Whatever was written between the component’s opening and closing tags
All the DOM nodes the component rendered
mcqs.explanation: `children` is an ordinary prop that JSX fills from the element body. It is what makes layout wrappers, providers and slots possible.

mcqs.question: Why can hooks not be called inside a condition or loop?
options: React identifies hooks by call order, so the order must be identical on every render
It is only a lint style preference
Because hooks are class methods internally
mcqs.explanation: React stores hook state in a per-component list indexed by call order. Skipping a hook on one render shifts every later hook onto the wrong slot. The single exception in React 19 is `use()`.

mcqs.question: When does the effect run?
options: Never — the dependency array is required
mcqs.explanation: No dependency array means "after every commit". `[]` means once after mount. `[a]` means whenever `a` changes by `Object.is`. The three cases are a favourite Mettl discrimination item.

mcqs.question: What is the returned function from `useEffect` for?
options: Cleanup — it runs before the next effect and on unmount
It is the value the effect produces for the component
It runs only on unmount, never between renders
Nothing — the return value is ignored
mcqs.explanation: Cleanup runs before the effect re-runs *and* at unmount. That is why subscriptions, intervals and listeners belong there — and why StrictMode’s double-invoke catches the ones that are missing.

mcqs.question: Which is TRUE of `useRef`?
options: Changing `.current` does not trigger a re-render
`useRef` recreates its object on every render
mcqs.explanation: A ref is a stable mutable box that survives renders and is invisible to the render cycle. That is exactly why it suits timer IDs, previous values and DOM handles — and why it must not hold anything the UI displays.

mcqs.question: `useCallback(fn, deps)` is equivalent to:
mcqs.explanation: `useCallback` memoises the function itself; `useMemo` memoises the result of calling something. Both exist to keep a **reference** stable across renders, usually for a `memo`’d child or a dependency array.

mcqs.question: Two components call the same custom hook `useCounter()`. What do they share?
options: Nothing — each call gets its own independent state
The same state, like a global store
Only the first mounted component gets state
mcqs.explanation: A custom hook shares *logic*, never state. Each call site gets its own hook slots. Sharing state needs context or a store — a very common interview trap.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between `useState(expensive())` and `useState(() => expensive())`?
options: The first calls `expensive()` on every render; the second only on the first render
mcqs.explanation: Arguments are evaluated before the call, so `useState(expensive())` runs the work every render and throws the result away. The lazy initialiser form runs it once. Same trap as inline objects in `memo` props.

mcqs.question: An effect with `[user]` where `user = { id }` is built inline in render. What happens?
options: The effect runs after every render, because the object identity changes each time
The effect runs only when `id` changes
React deep-compares objects in dependency arrays
mcqs.explanation: Dependencies are compared with `Object.is` — reference equality for objects. Depend on the primitive (`[user.id]`) or memoise the object. This is the single most common cause of infinite effect loops.

mcqs.question: A reducer must be a pure function. Which of these breaks that rule?
options: Calling `Date.now()` inside the reducer to stamp the new state
Returning a new object built with the spread operator
Returning the existing state unchanged for an unknown action
mcqs.explanation: A pure function returns the same output for the same input and causes no side effects. `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, API calls and mutation are all disqualifying — they make time-travel debugging and replay impossible.

mcqs.question: What is the correct Redux data flow?
options: dispatch(action) → reducer(state, action) → new store state → subscribed UI re-renders
Component mutates the store directly, then notifies the reducer
mcqs.explanation: Strictly unidirectional. The only way to change state is to dispatch an action; the only thing that computes new state is a reducer; the store is the single source of truth.

mcqs.question: What is the one required property of a Redux action?
mcqs.explanation: `type` is mandatory and should be a string constant. `payload`, `meta` and `error` are Flux Standard Action conventions, not requirements.

mcqs.question: What must a reducer return for an action it does not recognise?
mcqs.explanation: The `default` branch returns `state`. Returning `undefined` breaks the store; returning the initial state would wipe data every time any other slice’s action passed through.

mcqs.question: How many stores should a typical Redux application have?
options: One — a single source of truth, split into slices by `combineReducers`
mcqs.explanation: Redux mandates a single store. Modularity comes from combining reducers into slices of one state tree — this is a defining difference from Flux, which allows multiple stores.

mcqs.question: What do the two arguments of `connect(mapStateToProps, mapDispatchToProps)` do?
options: Select state slices as props, and bind action creators as props
Create the store, and create the reducer
Subscribe to routes, and to actions
Memoise the component, and its children
mcqs.explanation: `connect` is the classic HOC binding the store to a component. `mapStateToProps` reads; `mapDispatchToProps` writes. Hooks replaced it with `useSelector` / `useDispatch`, but the competency list still names `connect`.

mcqs.question: Why is middleware such as `redux-thunk` needed?
options: Reducers must stay pure, so asynchronous work has to happen outside them
mcqs.explanation: Middleware sits between `dispatch` and the reducer. Thunks let you dispatch a *function* that performs async work and dispatches plain actions when it resolves — keeping the reducer pure.

mcqs.question: What is wrong here?
options: It mutates state and returns the same reference, so subscribers see no change
Nothing — this is the standard pattern
mcqs.explanation: Two faults from one line: mutation (impure) and an unchanged reference (`===` comparison sees no update, so connected components never re-render). Correct: `return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.payload] }`.

mcqs.question: Which pair of store methods reads state and registers a listener?
mcqs.explanation: The store API is deliberately tiny: `getState`, `dispatch`, `subscribe`, `replaceReducer`. Everything else — `connect`, `useSelector` — is built on those four.

mcqs.question: `useSelector(state => ({ a: state.a, b: state.b }))` re-renders on every dispatch. Why?
options: It returns a new object each call, and the default comparison is reference equality
mcqs.explanation: `useSelector` compares the previous and next result with `===`. A fresh object literal never equals the last one. Fix: select primitives separately, or pass `shallowEqual` as the second argument.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between `createRoot` and `hydrateRoot`?
options: `createRoot` renders into empty DOM; `hydrateRoot` attaches to server-rendered HTML that already exists
`hydrateRoot` is the legacy API replaced by `createRoot`
`createRoot` is for class components, `hydrateRoot` for function components
They are aliases of each other
mcqs.explanation: `hydrateRoot` reuses existing server-rendered markup and attaches event handlers to it; mismatches produce hydration errors. `createRoot` (React 18+) replaced `ReactDOM.render` for client-only rendering.

mcqs.question: `useActionState` returns which tuple?
mcqs.explanation: It collapses the `useState` + `onSubmit` + loading-flag triad into one hook, and adds `isPending` as the third element. It was `useFormState` in canary and moved from `react-dom` to `react`.

mcqs.question: What does `useOptimistic` do?
options: Shows a temporary expected value immediately, then reconciles when the async action settles
Defers a state update to a lower priority
mcqs.explanation: It renders the optimistic value while an action is in flight and reverts or confirms when the real result lands — the "like button responds instantly" pattern, without hand-rolled rollback state.

mcqs.question: Where must a component calling `useFormStatus` sit?
options: Inside a `<form>` that has an action — it reads the parent form’s pending state
Anywhere; it reads global submission state
Directly in the component that owns the form state
mcqs.explanation: `useFormStatus` (from `react-dom`) lets a nested submit button read the enclosing form’s status without prop drilling or context — the point is that a shared `<SubmitButton>` needs no props.

mcqs.question: What makes `use()` unlike every other hook?
options: It can be called conditionally, and it reads promises as well as context
It may only be called at the top level of a Server Component
mcqs.explanation: `use()` reads a resource during render — a promise (suspending until it resolves) or a context — and is explicitly exempt from the top-level rule that binds every other hook.

mcqs.question: Which is TRUE of React Server Components?
options: They run on the server, ship no JavaScript to the client, and cannot use state or effects
They are client components rendered ahead of time
They can call `useState` as long as they are async
mcqs.explanation: RSCs execute on the server and stream a serialised result; they have no state, no effects and no browser APIs. Interactivity lives in client components marked `"use client"`. `"use server"` marks server actions.

mcqs.question: What changed about `ref` for function components in React 19?
options: `ref` can be passed as a normal prop — `forwardRef` is no longer required
`ref` was removed in favour of `useRef` only
Refs must now be objects, never callbacks
mcqs.explanation: React 19 lets function components accept `ref` directly in props, deprecating the `forwardRef` wrapper for new code. Callback refs also gained a cleanup return.

mcqs.question: What does this log?
mcqs.code: console.log([] == false, [] === false, !![]);
mcqs.explanation: `==` coerces: `[]` → `""` → `0`, and `false` → `0`, so it is `true`. `===` compares types first, so `false`. Every object is truthy, so `!![]` is `true` — an array is falsy in comparison and truthy in a condition.

mcqs.question: What is logged?
mcqs.code:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0);
mcqs.explanation: `var` is function-scoped — one binding, read after the loop finishes. `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration, which the closure captures. This is the classic closure item and it appears in almost every bank.

mcqs.question: What is logged?
mcqs.explanation: `this` is determined by the call site, not where the function was defined. Detaching the method loses the receiver — in a module (strict mode) `this` is `undefined`, so `this.n` is `undefined`. Fix with `bind`, an arrow wrapper, or a class field.

mcqs.question: What is the output order?
mcqs.explanation: Synchronous code first (A, D). Then the entire microtask queue — promise callbacks — drains (C). Only then does the event loop take a macrotask such as a timer (B). Microtasks always beat timers.

mcqs.question: What does an `async` function always return?
options: A Promise, whatever you return inside it
mcqs.explanation: `async` wraps the return value in a resolved promise and a thrown error in a rejected one. That is why the caller must `await` it or chain `.then`, and why `try/catch` inside works for awaited rejections.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes Flux from Redux?
options: Flux allows multiple stores and uses a central dispatcher; Redux has one store and no dispatcher
Flux is unidirectional, Redux is bidirectional
Flux uses reducers, Redux uses stores
They are the same library under different names
mcqs.explanation: Both are unidirectional. Flux has many stores coordinated by a singleton dispatcher; Redux collapses that to one store, pure reducers and no dispatcher object. Named on the vendor competency list despite being long out of fashion.

mcqs.question: In Webpack, what is a loader?
options: A transform applied to a file as it is added to the bundle — e.g. `babel-loader` for JSX
A plugin that runs after the bundle is written
The entry point of the application
A cache of previously built modules
mcqs.explanation: Loaders transform individual files during the build (JSX → JS, SCSS → CSS). Plugins act on the whole compilation (HTML generation, define, split-chunks). Confusing the two is the classic Webpack item.

mcqs.question: Which hook reads the dynamic segment of `/user/:id` in React Router?
mcqs.explanation: `useParams` returns path parameters; `useSearchParams` handles the query string; `useLocation` gives the whole location object; `useNavigate` performs navigation.

mcqs.question: `React.lazy(() => import("./X"))` must be rendered inside which component?
mcqs.explanation: A lazy component suspends while its chunk downloads, so it needs a `Suspense` boundary to render a fallback. An error boundary handles a *failed* chunk load — a different job.

mcqs.question: Which does NOT cause a component to re-render?
options: A `useState` setter called with a new value
A context value it consumes changing
mcqs.explanation: Refs are deliberately outside the render cycle. The other three are exactly the three causes of a re-render: own state, parent render, consumed context.

mcqs.question: A context provider passes `value={{ user, setUser }}`. Why do all consumers re-render on every provider render?
options: The object literal is a new reference every render
mcqs.explanation: Context compares the value by reference. A fresh literal breaks every consumer’s bail-out. Wrap it in `useMemo` keyed on the real dependencies — or split read and write into two contexts.

mcqs.question: What makes an input "controlled"?
options: Its `value` comes from React state and changes only through `onChange`
mcqs.explanation: Controlled = React state is the single source of truth. `defaultValue` plus a ref is the uncontrolled pattern, where the DOM owns the value. Passing `value` with no `onChange` produces a read-only input and a React warning.

mcqs.question: React’s `onClick` is:
options: A synthetic event — React attaches a listener at the root and delegates
A direct DOM listener attached to that exact element
An inline HTML attribute compiled into the markup
Only available on native HTML elements in class components
mcqs.explanation: React uses a synthetic event system with delegation at the root container (the app root since React 17, `document` before that). This normalises cross-browser behaviour and keeps listener count low.

mcqs.question: An element has `width: 200px; padding: 16px; border: 2px solid`. How wide is it on screen with the default `box-sizing`?
mcqs.explanation: Default `content-box` means `width` sizes the content only: 200 + 16×2 + 2×2 = 236. `box-sizing: border-box` makes 200 the total — which is why the universal reset exists.

mcqs.question: Which is the correct semantic element for the primary navigation links?
mcqs.explanation: Semantic elements carry implicit ARIA roles: `<nav>` is a navigation landmark screen readers can jump to. `<section>` needs a heading to be meaningful; `<aside>` is complementary content.

mcqs.question: You need rows AND columns to align across the whole layout. Which is the right tool?
options: Flexbox — it handles both axes at once
mcqs.explanation: Flexbox lays out along one axis at a time and is content-driven; Grid defines both axes on the parent, so tracks line up across rows and columns. "One axis or two" is the whole decision.
